Today a friend who was driving a load past this area stopped to lend a hand. He brought a shovel and some 2x6 boards. My lazy plan had intended he back his truck up to the edge across the wash and tow me out. His truck got stuck before he even got position. He wasn't even in the wash, but the crust is thin and the sand underneath unforgiving. Luckily we had a shovel and some 2x6 boards to help dig him out.

He was working and although he offered to help dig me out after we got him back to the safety of the hard packed truck trail - our quick success in getting him out put some wind back in my bag and instead I simply asked for a ride back into town with my cooler. We also dumped all my trash in a dumpster which made me feel better about having one less pile of problem to repack and shift as I extracate. We stopped for various applications of Carne Asade and the only thing I regret is not picking up a cheap bottle of Whiskey in town. But there will be burgers for me and dog the next day so it isn't all bad. Also I have luke warm Monster to look forward to tomorrow.

I put the boards and shovel to use and got the truck 3/4 of the way turned around. Still on the wrong side of the wash, and still with the trailer to contend with, but significant progress. Having positioned onto the boards for what I thought would be my last digging session before getting completely back on the road, my thoughts turned to how I would traverse the wash. A pile of railroad ties about 1/4 mile away seem like a good way to make a crossing.

But as if reading my thoughts - my power steering went out. Quick investigation found that both the power steering and alternator belts had derailed. The brand new belts I had professionally installed at the beginning of the trip. I have no explanation, but with the Chiltons manual I'm confident I can get them back on before quitting for the night.

Yesterday after enlisting the help, I took the afternoon to hike up into the hills nearby and survey the valley. It seems that it should be dry out here but some washes have moss growing on their banks and many of the plants and cacti have lovely blooms. Yellow, Purple, Violet, and a rare Dark Red are all present. Unlike the sickeningly sweet smell of store bought flowers, there is nothing overwhelming here.

The dog seriously lagged behind, hugging shade whenever possible. It is obvious he is no good in the heat - normally on our walks he bursts ahead and needs to be called back. Now I was stopping to wait for him to catch up, but then he was gone.

I hadn't brought any water but the hike was only an hour or so. But he was gone. I climbed felled trees and yelled for him. Gone. My initial concern for the hike had been rattlesnakes, so I had brought my trusty +5 Int Wizard Staff/Hiking stick and my +3 Dex sidearm. No sign of snakes. As I frantically made a fan pattern in search for the next few hours I imagined him finding a den of the coyotes we hear crying at night. He would have tried to play with them but I saw them in my minds eye saying 'homey don't play that' with a Southwestern accent and mobbing him like an LA gang.

Checking back at camp he wasn't there either and my heart sunk and dragged along behind me as I returned back into the desert looking for tracks. I brought water and finally after 3 or 4 hours finally heard panting in response to my constant calling. He had either just lay down and given up due to heat exhaustion or followed the wrong shady wash. I cut the jug of water into a bowl and he drank it all.
